timeline.title: Augustinian Missions and the Visita of Catuguian
timeline.description: Augustinian missionaries set up a mission in Gapan in 1595, which led to a Cabanatuan visita in 1750. Cabanatuan became a cabecera in 1780, and in 1846 Catuguian, then a barrio of Cabanatuan, became a visita of its mission.

timeline.title: Nueva Ecija Becomes a Province
timeline.description: Nueva Ecija was organized as a district (corregimiento) in 1801 and became an independent, regular province in 1848. Catuguian's population grew afterwards.

timeline.title: Catuguian Becomes an Independent Pueblo
timeline.description: Catuguian residents petitioned the alcalde-mayor of Nueva Ecija for a town. It was granted on December 11, 1852, with Catuguian as cabecera. The first barrios were La Torre, Santo Domingo (Pulong Buli), Baloc, Concepcion and Valle.

timeline.title: Catuguian Renamed Talavera
timeline.description: A petition filed on February 4 asked to rename the town after Talavera de la Reina in Spain. It was approved on February 14.

timeline.title: Education, Growth and Parish Recognition
timeline.description: A royal decree of 20 December 1863 established separate primary schools for boys and girls in each pueblo. By 1866 the population was 4,421. On November 20, 1872, a Royal Decree by King Amadeo I recognized the Parroquia de Talavera as an independent parish. Extensive grasslands also made Talavera a major cattle supplier for Manila.

timeline.title: Occupation by General Lawton
timeline.description: During the Philippine-American War, Talavera was occupied by American General Henry Lawton.

timeline.title: Territorial Adjustments
timeline.description: Sitio Bacal was annexed in 1910 (Executive Order No. 39, s. 1909). Eight sitios were separated in 1912 to form Muñoz (EO No. 72). Barrio Lomboy was annexed in 1914 (EO No. 25). Barrio San Francisco went to Santo Domingo in 1937 (EO No. 96).

timeline.title: Haciendas and Tenancy Conflicts
timeline.description: Migration increased as haciendas and cattle grazing expanded. Peasant struggles over landlordism and shared tenancy appeared in San Ricardo, Bantug, Casili and Morcon.

timeline.title: Japanese Occupation and Birth of Squadron 8
timeline.description: The Imperial Japanese Army occupied Talavera in December 1941. Hukbalahap Squadron 8 was formed in Talavera with more than 100 members.

timeline.title: Defense Line and Rescue of 510 Prisoners
timeline.description: San Pascual and Pinagpanaan became a strategic defense line against the retreating Japanese army. Barangay Sibul served as a rendezvous point for 510 rescued prisoners of war from Camp Pangatian.

timeline.title: Post-War Huk Expansion
timeline.description: After the war, Huk forces expanded in Nueva Ecija, in what was known as 'Huklandia'. Talavera was part of this area.

timeline.title: Barrios Annexed to Llanera
timeline.description: General Luna, Morcon, Mabini, Ricarte, Casili and Picon, along with Plaridel and Bosque, were annexed to the new municipality of Llanera under Republic Act 1221.

timeline.title: Ang Kasaysayan ng Talavera
timeline.description: Mayor Romeo F. Maliwat commissioned public librarian Tomas I. Pagaduan to compile Talavera's history. It was published in 1967 and is likely the best local primary source.

facts.title: Named After a Spanish City
facts.description: In 1853, Catuguian was renamed Talavera after Talavera de la Reina in Spain.

facts.title: Manila's Cattle Supplier
facts.description: Under Spanish rule, Talavera's extensive grasslands made it a major cattle supplier for the Manila market.

facts.title: Dispute with Science City of Muñoz
facts.description: From 1996 to 1999, Muñoz claimed four Talavera barangays (Bakal I, II, III and Matingkis), but the claim was set aside in March 1999 and they stayed with Talavera.

facts.title: Linggo ng Magsasaka
facts.description: A week-long celebration honoring Talavera's farmers, ending on the May 15 town fiesta with dance contests, a float parade and the Kesong Puti Festival.

facts.title: Gatas ng Kalabaw Festival
facts.description: Talavera has hosted this festival promoting carabao's milk, with street dancing, a carabao race and a milk drinking contest.

facts.title: Semana Santa and the Cofradia
facts.description: During Holy Week, parish members bring their own saint images, set on decorated carrozas, to the Holy Wednesday and Good Friday processions.
